Hi Raj / Elena - thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we stay aligned and unblock the technical deep-dive:

Summary of requirements (please correct if I mis-stated):
- Latency SLOs: p95 <= 200ms for interactive flows; p99 target around ~800ms-1s for heavier prompts.
- Throughput & concurrency: baseline 300 req/s sustained, with spikes to ~800 req/s during peak windows; concurrent streaming sessions ~350 typical, up to ~500 at peaks.
- Streaming: low-latency token streaming required (clients render tokens as they arrive). We need to preserve per-stream order and support graceful cancellation.
- Burst/autoscale expectations: need capacity to absorb spikes to 800 req/s with scale-up time ideally <60s to reach warm capacity; cold start fallback acceptable but must not violate SLOs for more than a short window.

Open questions for you:
1) Can you confirm the expected peak duration (minutes vs hours) and whether spikes are predictable by schedule?
2) Are you comfortable with a warm-pool sizing approach (some reserved warm workers + burst autoscale) vs fully reserved capacity?
3) Any constraints around cost vs latency trade-offs we should be aware of?

Next steps: attaching a short SLO template (fastpay_slo_requirements.pdf) that we use to lock targets internally - if you can fill/confirm, Connor and I will map that to an autoscale + warm-pool recommendation and schedule a 45m technical deep-dive with Dylan.

Hi all - looping in some technical notes to answer the warm-pool / autoscale cost trade-off and how Redwood behaves under spike. TL;DR: warm pools keep p95 tight during spikes with predictable cost; autoscale with cold starts works but will expose some higher tail latency during spin-up.

Key behavior and knobs:
- Warm pools: we can reserve a small set of pre-warmed workers (GPU instances with model loaded + KV cache primed) that can be scaled up/down. For a target burst of 800 req/s we typically size warm pool to handle ~40-60% of expected burst (so it responds immediately) and rely on autoscale to fill the remainder.
- Scale-up times: moving from warm worker ready -> serving is typically <30s. Cold start (new instance + model load) can be 2-4 minutes depending on model size and quantization.
- Queueing/fallback: Redwood will queue excess requests briefly (configurable max queue time) and can return degraded responses or fall back to a smaller model variant to preserve latency SLOs. We recommend setting a short max queue (15-30s) and a fallback policy to a cheaper-compatible model for non-critical flows.
- Concurrency model: per-worker concurrency depends on model and kernel optimization; for the Llama-variant you mentioned we expect ~6-8 concurrent streams per worker for target latency bounds.

Attachment: redwood_warmpool_design.png - simple diagram showing warm pool + autoscale flow.

Proposed concrete next steps for the deep-dive:
1) You send back the filled SLO template (Marissa)
2) We run a quick traffic replay (using fastpay_traffic_spike.csv) against a staging autoscale config to measure real scale-up behavior (30-90 minutes)
3) Technical call to review measured numbers and lock warm-pool sizing + queue policies (45 minutes)

Happy to join either proposed time (tomorrow or Fri afternoon PT).

- Dylan
